newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Westpac says hard to match first half.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Westpac says hard to match first half.

text.p: Westpac Banking Corp said on Wednesday it would be hard to repeat its first half profit growth in the second half ending September 30.
"I think that it will be very hard to do in the second half given the margin pressures that we're seeing going through the marketplace," Westpac Managing Director Bob Joss told a news conference.
He had been asked whether Westpac could repeat the 12.9 percent profit growth posted in the first half.
Joss said he expected the full year profit for 1996/97 would be higher than the A$1.132 billion posted in 1995/96.
"I would hope and expect that we would do better in year 1997 than we did in year 1996. That's currently what we are striving for," he said.

Joss said the rise in net profit to A$638 million in the six months to March 31 from A$565 million in the corresponding six months a year earlier was very solid, particularly given the margin pressures evident in home lending in particular.

He said the fall in Westpac's group net interest margin to 3.55 percent in the six months to March 31 from 3.76 percent in the six months to September 30 had cost Westpac about A$88 million, which in turn was passed on as a benefit to consumers.
Westpac's increases in bank fees and charges had not fully offset the effect of this margin squeeze, he said.
"There was no way that we had fee increases of that magnitude," he said.
Westpac's accounts for the first half released earlier showed Westpac's account keeping and transaction fee income rose to A$379 million from A$306 million a year earlier.
"There's constant pressure on margins so there's a test to do the best we can on fees, on lowering costs and increasing efficiencies," Joss said.
Joss agreed that a portion of the profit increase had come from property sale profits, "which tend to be lumpy."
Westpac's accounts showed profits on sales of premises and investments rose to A$60 million from A$9 million.

The combination of higher fee income and property profits make up A$124 million of the A$155 million improvement in overall non-interest income, which was itself the driving factor in the higher profit.
Meanwhile Joss described Westpac's announcement of a possible A$500 million converting preference share issue as an insurance policy to keep the group's balance sheet strong.
The preference share issue would only be needed if a large number of Bank of Melbourne Ltd shareholders decided not to take up Westpac's share plus cash offer and took the cash only offer.
Westpac offered one of its shares plus A$1.85 in cash per Bank of Melbourne share or A$8.85 cash.
Some analysts have said that if Westpac's cash-only offer was fully taken up, Westpac's tier one capital adequacy ratio would drop below six percent, which is seen as a minimum acceptable ratio.
Westpac's tier one ratio stood at 7.7 percent at March 31.
Joss denied that a full cash take-up by Bank of Melbourne shareholders would cut tier one capital to below six percent.
He said Westpac would not hesitate to undertake the converting preference share issue if the tier one ratio went below a certain band. He would not specify the band.
He said however he would feel comfortable with the tier one ratio being below seven percent, but above 6.5 percent.
"There's certainly a range of 6.5 percent to seven percent that seems comfortable and we need to keep it there to keep our credit rating," he said.
Joss said there had been a high share take-up percentage by Challenge Bank Ltd shareholders in Westpac's successful takeover of Challenge in 1995.
Westpac's share price closed down five cents at A$7.45 on Wednesday.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
